What friends and family are like; what makes a good friend.
Interests and socialising with friends and family.
Role models.
Study in the context of both the home country and Arabic-speaking communities.

Food and drink.
Shopping.

units.title: Business objectives
points: Financial aims include survival, profit, sales, market share and financial security
Non-financial aims include social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence and control
Objectives change with market conditions, technology, performance, legislation and internal reasons

units.title: Types of organisation
points: Sole traders, partnerships, private and public limited companies and public corporations
Compare forms by risk, ownership, limited liability, control, finance and use of profits
Stakeholders and shareholders; judging which ownership form suits a business
Franchises, social enterprises and multinationals

units.title: Classification of businesses
points: Primary sector businesses extract resources
Secondary sector businesses convert materials into goods
Tertiary sector businesses provide services

units.title: Location decisions
points: Location depends on proximity to market, labour, materials and competitors
The nature of the activity shapes the location choice
The internet allows e-commerce instead of fixed premises
Legal controls and trade blocs influence where a business locates

units.title: Market research
points: Research identifies customer needs and market gaps and reduces risk
Primary methods: surveys, questionnaires, focus groups, observation, test marketing
Secondary sources: internet, market reports, government reports
Qualitative and quantitative data, social media and reliability of results

units.title: The market
points: Marketing meets customer needs and builds relationships and loyalty
Market orientation versus product orientation; niche versus mass marketing
Businesses respond to changing needs, spending patterns and competition
Segmentation by location, demographics, lifestyle, income and age

units.title: Marketing mix
points: Product: new product development, goods versus services, packaging, life cycle, extension strategies, Boston matrix
Price: cost-plus, penetration, competition, skimming and promotional pricing
Place: retailers and e-tailers (e-commerce)
Promotion: advertising, sponsorship, trials, offers, branding, above and below the line, PR
Online promotion: targeted advertising, viral social media marketing and e-newsletters

units.title: Communication
points: Good communication matters to a business
Communication methods, including IT, have benefits and limitations
Barriers to communication and how to remove them

units.title: Recruitment and selection
points: Employment types: full-time, part-time, job share, casual, seasonal, temporary
Documents: job description, person specification, application form, CV
Internal versus external recruitment; advertising, shortlisting, interviewing
Legal controls: equal opportunities and minimum wage

units.title: Training
points: Training matters to the business and to workers
Induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training
Training supports health and safety compliance; benefits and limitations

units.title: Motivation and rewards
points: Motivation helps attract and retain staff and raises productivity
Theories of Herzberg, Maslow and Taylor
Financial methods: remuneration, bonus, commission, promotion, fringe benefits
Non-financial methods: job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy

units.title: Organisation structure and employees
points: Hierarchical versus flat structures; centralised versus decentralised decisions
Span of control, chain of command and delegation
Functional areas: human resources, finance, marketing and production

units.title: Sources of finance
points: Finance needs are short-term or long-term, for start-up or expansion
Internal sources: personal savings, retained profit, selling assets
External sources: overdrafts, trade payables, loans, share capital and flotation
Venture capital and crowdfunding

units.title: Cash flow forecasting
points: Cash pays suppliers, overheads and employees; shortages risk insolvency
Cash and profit are different things
Calculate and interpret inflows, outflows, net cash flow, opening and closing balances

units.title: Costs and break-even
points: Revenue, fixed costs, variable costs, total costs, profit and loss
Break-even output by formula or diagram
Interpret charts and the effect of changes in revenue and costs; know limitations

units.title: Financial documents
points: Statement of comprehensive income: sales, cost of sales, gross profit, expenses, operating profit
Statement of financial position: current and non-current assets and liabilities, capital employed
Candidates interpret these documents but do not construct them

units.title: Accounts analysis
points: Ratios: gross and operating profit margin, markup, ROCE, current ratio, acid test ratio
Judge liquidity and compare over time or with other businesses
Use financial documents to assess performance and inform decisions

units.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
points: Internal and external economies of scale
Diseconomies and the limits of growth

units.title: Production, lean production and technology
points: Job, batch and flow production; labour- versus capital-intensive methods
Calculate productivity and the effect of improving it
Lean production: just-in-time, Kaizen and effective use of resources
Technology such as robotics: balancing cost, productivity, quality and flexibility

units.title: Factors of production
points: Enterprise, capital, land and labour as factors of production
How their relationships change; capital-intensive versus labour-intensive activity

units.title: Quality
points: Quality matters for goods and services
Quality control and total quality management (TQM)
Quality as a source of competitive advantage

units.title: Business and the international economy
points: Globalisation: concept, opportunities and threats
Multinationals: benefits to the firm, and benefits and drawbacks for host countries
Calculate exchange rate conversions
Exchange rate changes affect competitiveness, importers and exporters

units.title: Government objectives and policies
points: Government spending on public services; taxation and limits on spending
Infrastructure, legislation and trade policy such as trading blocs and tariffs
Interest rate changes affect businesses and consumer spending

units.title: External factors
points: Social, technological, environmental and political influences on business decisions

units.title: Business success
points: Success measures: revenue, market share, customer satisfaction, profit, growth, owner and employee satisfaction
Failure reasons: cash flow or lack of finance, uncompetitive, failure to adapt

units.title: Computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction and subprograms
points: Explain how decomposition and abstraction help model and solve problems (1.1.1).
Explain the benefits of using subprograms (1.1.2).

units.title: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
points: Follow and write algorithms with sequence, selection, repetition and iteration over data structures (1.2.1).
Use variables, constants, strings, records and one- and two-dimensional arrays (1.2.2).
Use arithmetic, relational and logical operators (1.2.3).
Work out outputs and variable values using trace tables (1.2.4).
Identify syntax, logic and runtime errors and correct logic errors (1.2.5).
Explain how bubble sort, merge sort, linear search and binary search work (1.2.6).
Judge fitness for purpose and efficiency using test data (1.2.7).

units.title: Computational thinking: logic and truth tables
points: Complete and interpret truth tables using AND, OR and NOT, with up to three inputs (1.3.1).
Write and read logic expressions and relate them to program conditions (1.3.1).

units.title: Data: binary and number representation
points: Binary represents data and instructions; count the states available for a given number of bits (2.1.1).
Represent unsigned integers and signed integers using two's complement (2.1.2).
Convert between denary and 8-bit binary: 0 to 255, and -128 to +127 (2.1.3).
Add positive binary numbers and apply logical and arithmetic shifts (2.1.4).
Explain overflow when a result exceeds the available bits (2.1.5).
Explain why hexadecimal is used and convert between hex and binary (2.1.6).

units.title: Data: representing text, images and sound
points: Represent characters using 7-bit ASCII (2.2.1).
Describe bitmap images using pixels, resolution and colour depth (2.2.2).
Describe sound sampling using amplitude, sample rate, bit depth and sample interval (2.2.3).
Explain the limits of binary representation when the number of bits is fixed (2.2.4).

units.title: Data: storage units and compression
points: Use binary storage units from bit to tebibyte; calculate file sizes and capacities (2.3.1).
Explain why compression is needed and compare lossless and lossy methods (2.3.2).

units.title: Computers: architecture, memory and storage
points: Describe the von Neumann stored-program concept, RAM, CPU components, clock, buses and the fetch-decode-execute cycle (3.1.1).
Explain how magnetic, optical and solid-state secondary storage store data (3.1.2).
Describe embedded systems and their uses (3.1.3).

units.title: Computers: operating systems, utilities and robust software
points: Describe operating system functions: file, process, peripheral and user management (3.2.1).
Describe utility software: repair, backup, compression, defragmentation and anti-malware (3.2.2).
Explain robust software and finding vulnerabilities through audit trails and code reviews (3.2.3).

units.title: Computers: programming languages and translators
points: Compare the characteristics and purposes of low-level and high-level languages (3.3.1).
Explain how interpreters and compilers translate high-level code differently (3.3.2).

units.title: Networks: types, protocols and connections
points: Give reasons for connecting computers in networks (4.1.1).
Distinguish LAN and WAN (4.1.2).
Describe internet structure, including IP addressing and routers (4.1.3).
Explain how wired and wireless connections affect speed, range, latency and bandwidth (4.1.4).
Calculate transmission time, rate and file size from network speed in bits per second (4.1.5).
Describe protocols: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, POP3, SMTP and IMAP (4.1.6).
Describe the four-layer TCP/IP model (4.1.7).
Compare bus, star and mesh topologies (4.1.8).

units.title: Networks: network security
points: Identify network vulnerabilities through penetration testing and ethical hacking (4.2.1).
Explain protections: access control, physical security and firewalls (4.2.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: environmental effects
points: Discuss environmental impacts of computing: energy use, manufacture, replacement cycles and disposal (5.1.1).
Weigh the environmental costs of devices against their benefits when giving a reasoned view (5.1.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: ethical, legal and ownership issues
points: Discuss ethics and law of personal data: privacy, consent, ownership, misuse and data protection (5.2.1).
Discuss AI, machine learning and robotics: accountability, safety, algorithmic bias and liability (5.2.2).
Explain intellectual property: copyright, patents, trademarks and licensing (5.2.3).

units.title: Issues and impact: cybersecurity
points: Describe malware types, technical vulnerabilities and social engineering (5.3.1).
Explain protection methods: anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery (5.3.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: designing, reading and refining programs
points: Use decomposition and abstraction to solve problems (6.1.1).
Read, write, analyse and refine high-level programs (6.1.2).
Convert flowcharts and pseudocode into programs (6.1.3).
Write readable code: layout, indentation, comments, meaningful names and whitespace (6.1.4).
Find and correct logic, syntax and runtime errors (6.1.5).
Evaluate fitness for purpose and efficiency using test data (6.1.6).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: program structure and control
points: Identify the structural components of a program (6.2.1).
Use sequence, selection, repetition and iteration, each with a single entry and exit point (6.2.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: data types, variables and strings
points: Use primitive types (integer, real, Boolean, character) and one- and two-dimensional structures (6.3.1).
Use variables and constants (6.3.2).
Manipulate strings: length, position, substrings and case conversion (6.3.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: input, files, validation and authentication
points: Accept and respond to user input (6.4.1).
Read from and write to CSV text files (6.4.2).
Apply validation: length, presence, range and pattern checks (6.4.3).
Apply authentication: ID and password, and lookup (6.4.4).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: operators
points: Use arithmetic operators, including modulus, integer division and exponentiation (6.5.1).
Use relational operators (6.5.2).
Use logical operators AND, OR and NOT (6.5.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: subprograms and scope
points: Use built-in, library and user-defined subprograms (6.6.1).
Know that functions return values and procedures do not (6.6.2).
Use global and local variables appropriately (6.6.3).

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 1, retrieval
points: Short-form question worth 4 marks, based on a stated range of lines in the extract.
Skill: identify and interpret explicit information and ideas (AO1).
Answers may quote or paraphrase; copying out a long section earns no credit.
Reading is of one 20th or 21st century prose fiction extract, printed on the paper.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 2, language
points: 8 marks, on a short stated part of the extract.
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to create effects (AO2).
Bullet points on the paper are guidance only and carry no marks.
Subject terminology is credited, from simple to sophisticated use, but analysis of effect matters most.
The same skill is assessed again in Paper 2 Q3.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 3, structure
points: 8 marks, on the structure of the whole extract.
Skill: analyse how the writer has organised the text for effect (AO2).
Advice: write in detail about two or three well-chosen structural features.
Sentence-level analysis counts only where it helps explain the structure of the whole text.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 4, evaluation
points: Extended question worth 20 marks, the largest reading question on Paper 1.
Skill: evaluate the text critically, supported by textual references (AO4).
A statement is given and students decide how far they agree with it.
Marks reward the quality of evaluation, not which position is taken.
Responses may cover the writer's methods and the reader's response, with evidence.

units.title: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended task: describe or narrate, from a written prompt or an image.
The statement before the task sets the audience and purpose.
Marked on tone, style and register, plus organisation for coherence and cohesion.
Marked on vocabulary range, sentence variety, spelling and punctuation.
Notional 15 minutes of reading time is built into the 1 hour 45 minutes; leave time to check.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1, true statements
points: 4 marks: choose the four true statements from a list that mixes true and false ones.
Skill: identify explicit and implicit information (AO1) in a stated part of Source A.
If more than four are chosen, only the first four in order are marked.
Two linked sources: one non-fiction and one literary non-fiction, from different periods including the 19th century.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 2, summary
points: 8 marks: a summary of the differences or similarities between the two sources, on a stated focus.
Skill: select relevant information and synthesise it across both texts (AO1).
Write in continuous prose, drawing inferences rather than listing quotations.
Use only material that answers the specific focus given in the question.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
points: 12 marks, on one source only (in the specimen, the 19th-century letter).
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to influence the reader (AO2).
Same skill as Paper 1 Q2, applied to non-fiction and literary non-fiction.
Subject terminology supports analysis of effect but does not replace it.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
points: Extended question worth 16 marks, using the whole of both sources.
Skill: compare writers' ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed (AO3).
Comparison should go beyond basic comprehension to methods: language and structure.
Both sources need balanced, supported coverage, with linking comparative language.

units.title: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended piece presenting the student's own view on a statement or theme linked to Section A.
Audience, purpose and form are stated (the specimen asks for a newspaper article).
Material from Section A may be used, but as the student's own view of it.
Rewards persuasive organisation, controlled register, varied sentences and accurate spelling and punctuation.

units.title: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
points: A formal presentation of no more than about ten minutes, on a topic agreed with the teacher.
Students respond to questions and feedback from the audience (AO8).
Spoken Standard English must be used effectively and be audible and intelligible (AO9).
Graded Pass, Merit or Distinction on a competency basis; all criteria for a grade must be met.
Reported separately on the certificate; carries no marks and no weighting in the GCSE grade.

units.title: Subject content: reading across the course
points: Read fluently and critically a wide range of 19th, 20th and 21st century texts.
Texts include literature, literary non-fiction, reviews and journalism.
Evaluate and compare texts, and summarise and synthesise ideas across them.
Use reading to inform the student's own writing.

units.title: Subject content: writing across the course
points: Write clearly and coherently in Standard English for different purposes and audiences.
Purposes named: describing, narrating, explaining, instructing, informing, arguing.
Use accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling, and a wide vocabulary.
Use rhetorical and creative techniques for impact.

units.title: Component 1 Section A: Unseen poetry
points: One 20-mark essay question on a poem not seen before, assessed for AO2.
Candidates also study a selection of modern poetry to prepare for it.
Focus is language, form and structure and the effects they create.
Closed-book paper, so no prepared quotations are possible for this section.

units.title: Component 1 Section B: Anthology poetry (16 poems)
points: Part 3 of the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Anthology; all 16 poems are studied.
One 30-mark question from a choice of two, assessed for AO2 and AO3.
Questions ask candidates to compare poems; a clean copy of the poems is supplied.
Poems come from different periods and cultures, so links and connections between texts are credited.

units.title: Anthology poems 1 to 8
points: If- (Rudyard Kipling).
Prayer Before Birth (Louis MacNeice).
Blessing (Imtiaz Dharker).
Search For My Tongue (Sujata Bhatt).
Half-past Two (U A Fanthorpe).
Piano (D H Lawrence).
Hide and Seek (Vernon Scannell).
Sonnet 116: Let me not to the marriage of true minds (William Shakespeare).

units.title: Anthology poems 9 to 16
points: La Belle Dame sans Merci (John Keats).
Poem at Thirty-Nine (Alice Walker).
War Photographer (Carol Ann Duffy).
The Tyger (William Blake).
My Last Duchess (Robert Browning).
Half-caste (John Agard).
Do not go gentle into that good night (Dylan Thomas).
Remember (Christina Rossetti).

units.title: Component 1 Section C: Modern prose (choose one text)
points: One 40-mark question from a choice of two on the chosen prose text.
Assessed for AO1 (knowledge and personal engagement) and AO4 (context).
Closed book; the examiner report shows questions on theme, character and significance.
Context is credited where it relates to how the text was written and received.

units.title: Modern prose options listed by Pearson Edexcel
points: To Kill a Mockingbird (Harper Lee).
Of Mice and Men (John Steinbeck).
The Whale Rider (Witi Ihimaera).
The Joy Luck Club (Amy Tan).
Things Fall Apart (Chinua Achebe).
Klara and the Sun (Kazuo Ishiguro): new, first assessment May 2026.
Western Lane (Chetna Maroo): new, first assessment May 2026.

units.title: Component 2 or 3 Section A / Assignment A: Modern drama (choose one)
points: Component 2: one 30-mark question from a choice of two, open book, assessed for AO1 and AO2.
Component 3: internally assessed assignment of 30 marks (15 AO1, 15 AO2), externally moderated.
Drama is studied as a script for performance as well as a printed text.

units.title: Modern drama options listed by Pearson Edexcel
points: A View from the Bridge (Arthur Miller).
An Inspector Calls (J B Priestley).
The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time (Mark Haddon, adapted by Simon Stephens).
Kindertransport (Diane Samuels).
Death and the King's Horseman (Wole Soyinka).

units.title: Component 2 or 3 Section B / Assignment B: Literary heritage texts (choose one)
points: Component 2: one 30-mark question from a choice of two, open book, assessed for AO1, AO2 and AO4.
Component 3: assignment of 30 marks (10 each for AO1, AO2 and AO4), internally assessed.
Non-examined marks from both assignments combine into one mark out of 60.
Candidates relate the text to the context in which it was written.

units.title: Literary heritage options listed by Pearson Edexcel
points: Romeo and Juliet (William Shakespeare).
Macbeth (William Shakespeare).
The Merchant of Venice (William Shakespeare).
Pride and Prejudice (Jane Austen).
Great Expectations (Charles Dickens).
The Scarlet Letter (Nathaniel Hawthorne).

units.title: SCHOOL CHOICE: Macbeth (literary heritage text)
points: Macbeth is on the Pearson Edexcel literary heritage list, so the school text is permitted.
Existing Y11 lessons teach it as context and witches, then tyranny, guilt and downfall.
Existing lessons are written to the AQA 8702 exam format and need re-mapping.
Open-book Component 2 allows the text to be used, so quotation recall matters less.
Marks differ: 30 marks on AO1, AO2 and AO4 rather than extract plus whole-text format.

units.title: SCHOOL CHOICE: A Christmas Carol (not on the Pearson list)
points: A Christmas Carol does not appear in the Pearson Edexcel 4ET1 text lists.
Existing Y10 lessons on it are AQA 8702 material and cannot be assessed here.
It could remain as wider reading on Victorian society and Dickens, not as a set text.
Closest Pearson option for Dickens: Great Expectations in the literary heritage list.

gcse-science.subject: Science
gcse-science.code: Biology 4BI1; Chemistry 4CH1; Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0 (linear). No 4SD1 code was found.

units.title: The nature and variety of living organisms
units.paper: Biology Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Biology Paper 1
points: Living things share eight characteristics, from nutrition and respiration to growth and development.
Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi, protoctists) have common features, illustrated with examples.
Prokaryotes such as bacteria have common features, illustrated with examples.
Pathogens may be fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses; viruses are described as non-living particles.

units.title: Structure and functions in living organisms
units.paper: Biology Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Biology Paper 1
points: Organisation from organelle to system; plant and animal cell structures, functions, similarities and differences.
Differentiation, specialised cells and stem cell uses (Biology only, Paper 2).
Food tests, enzyme action, effects of temperature and pH on the active site; diffusion, osmosis, active transport.
Photosynthesis: equations, limiting factors, leaf structure, mineral needs; human diet, digestion, bile, villus.
Respiration makes ATP; aerobic and anaerobic equations; gas exchange in plants and in the human thorax.
Transport: xylem, phloem, transpiration; blood, immunity, heart, vessels, coronary heart disease risk.
Excretion: lungs, kidneys, skin; nephron, ultrafiltration and ADH in Biology only.
Co-ordination: stimulus, receptor, effector; plant tropisms and auxin; nervous system, reflex arc, eye.
Hormones: adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone; homeostasis and skin temperature control.
Practical points: food tests, enzyme temperature, diffusion and osmosis, photosynthesis, respiration, breathing, transpiration.

units.title: Reproduction and inheritance
units.paper: Biology Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Biology Paper 1
points: Sexual and asexual reproduction; flower structure, pollination, fertilisation, germination and artificial propagation.
Human reproductive systems, menstrual cycle hormones, placenta and secondary sexual characteristics.
Genome, genes and chromosomes; DNA double helix, base pairing and RNA (Biology only detail).
Protein synthesis by transcription and translation (Biology only).
Alleles, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype and phenotype; codominance in Biology only.
Monohybrid crosses, pedigrees, probability and sex determination by XX and XY.
Mitosis for growth and repair; meiosis makes haploid gametes; human diploid 46, haploid 23.
Variation is genetic and environmental; mutation is rare, random and inheritable; mutagens (Biology only).
Darwin's theory of natural selection; antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

units.title: Ecology and the environment
units.paper: Biology Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Biology Paper 1
points: Population, community, habitat and ecosystem; estimating population size with quadrats.
Biodiversity and distribution measured with quadrats (Biology only).
Abiotic and biotic factors affect population size and distribution.
Trophic levels, food chains, webs, and pyramids of number, biomass and energy; about 10% energy transfer.
Carbon cycle; nitrogen cycle with named bacteria (Biology only).
Pollution: sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, greenhouse gases, global warming, sewage and eutrophication.
Deforestation effects on soil, water and the carbon cycle (Biology only).

units.title: Use of biological resources
units.paper: Biology Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Biology Paper 1
points: Crop yield: glasshouses, polythene tunnels, carbon dioxide, temperature, fertilisers and pest control.
Micro-organisms: yeast in bread, Lactobacillus in yoghurt, industrial fermenters and their conditions.
Fish farming methods and problems (Biology only).
Selective breeding of plants and animals for desired traits.
Genetic engineering: restriction enzymes, ligase, plasmid and viral vectors; GM bacteria make human insulin.
Transgenic organisms and GM plants improving food production.
Cloning: micropropagation and nuclear transfer, including Dolly the sheep (Biology only).

units.title: Principles of chemistry
units.paper: Chemistry Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Chemistry Paper 1
points: States of matter, interconversions, diffusion, solute, solvent, saturated solution; solubility curves in Chemistry only.
Elements, compounds, mixtures; purity and melting point; separation methods and Rf from chromatograms.
Atomic structure: sub-atomic particles, atomic and mass number, isotopes, relative atomic mass calculations.
Periodic Table: groups, periods, electronic configurations of the first 20 elements, metals and non-metals.
Equations with state symbols; relative formula mass, moles, reacting masses and percentage yield.
Empirical and molecular formulae; concentration and molar gas volume in Chemistry only.
Ionic bonding: ion charges, formulae, dot-and-cross diagrams, lattice properties and conductivity.
Covalent bonding: dot-and-cross diagrams, simple molecules, giant structures (diamond, graphite, C60).
Metallic bonding and properties (Chemistry only).
Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes, half-equations, oxidation and reduction (Chemistry only).
Practical points: solubility, chromatography, metal oxide formula, electrolysis of aqueous solutions.

units.title: Inorganic chemistry
units.paper: Chemistry Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Chemistry Paper 1
points: Group 1 metals: reactions with water and air, predicting trends; electronic explanation in Chemistry only.
Group 7 halogens: colours, states, trends and displacement reactions.
Gases in air: percentage composition, finding oxygen content, metal carbonate decomposition, carbon dioxide as greenhouse gas.
Reactivity series from water, acid and displacement reactions; rusting, rust prevention, redox.
Extraction of metals linked to reactivity, uses of metals and alloys (Chemistry only).
Acids, alkalis, pH scale, indicators and titration (titration in Chemistry only).
Solubility rules, acids and bases as proton donors and acceptors; preparing soluble and insoluble salts.
Tests for gases, flame colours, cations (ammonium, copper, iron), anions (halides, sulfate, carbonate) and water.
Practical points: air composition, acid with metals, copper(II) sulfate crystals, lead(II) sulfate.

units.title: Physical chemistry
units.paper: Chemistry Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Chemistry Paper 1
points: Exothermic and endothermic reactions; calorimetry, Q = mcDeltaT and molar enthalpy change.
Energy level diagrams and bond energy calculations (Chemistry only).
Rates of reaction: surface area, concentration, pressure, temperature and catalysts explained by collision theory.
Catalysts give a lower activation energy pathway; reaction profile diagrams (Chemistry only).
Reversible reactions and the reversible symbol with examples.
Dynamic equilibrium and effects of temperature and pressure on position (Chemistry only).
Practical points: temperature changes, marble chips and acid, catalysts with hydrogen peroxide.

units.title: Organic chemistry
units.paper: Chemistry Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Chemistry Paper 1
points: Hydrocarbons, formulae types, homologous series, functional groups, isomerism and IUPAC naming to six carbons.
Crude oil: fractional distillation, fractions and their uses, trends in boiling point and viscosity.
Complete and incomplete combustion, carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen, sulfur dioxide and acid rain.
Catalytic cracking and why it is needed to match supply and demand.
Alkanes are saturated and react with halogens in UV light; alkenes are unsaturated.
Bromine addition and the bromine water test separate alkenes from alkanes.
Alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters: structures, oxidation, manufacture and fermentation (Chemistry only).
Addition polymers: monomers, repeat units and disposal problems.
Condensation polymers and biopolyesters (Chemistry only); ester preparation practical.

units.title: Forces and motion
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: SI units; distance-time and velocity-time graphs, gradient as acceleration, area as distance.
Average speed, acceleration and the equation v squared = u squared + 2as.
Vectors and scalars, resultant force, F = ma and W = mg.
Stopping distance, its factors, falling objects and terminal velocity.
Force-extension graphs, Hooke's law and elastic behaviour.
Momentum, conservation of momentum, force as rate of change of momentum, Newton's third law (Physics only).
Moments, centre of gravity and the principle of moments (Physics only).

units.title: Electricity
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Units and mains electricity: insulation, earthing, fuses, circuit breakers, a.c. and d.c.
Power P = IV, energy E = IVt and choosing fuses.
Series and parallel circuits, current conserved at junctions, V = IR and Q = It.
Current-voltage behaviour of resistors, filament lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors.
Voltage as energy per charge, E = QV; current as flow of electrons.
Electric charge, charging by friction, uses and dangers of static (Physics only).

units.title: Waves
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Longitudinal and transverse waves; amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period; v = f x wavelength and f = 1/T.
Waves transfer energy not matter; Doppler effect; reflection and refraction.
Electromagnetic spectrum order, shared speed, uses and hazards of each region.
Ray diagrams, law of reflection, refractive index n = sin i / sin r.
Total internal reflection, critical angle, sin c = 1/n and optical fibres.
Sound as a longitudinal wave; hearing range, speed of sound, oscilloscope traces, pitch and loudness (Physics only).

units.title: Energy resources and energy transfers
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Energy stores and transfers, conservation of energy, efficiency and Sankey diagrams.
Conduction, convection and radiation; reducing unwanted thermal transfer.
Work done W = Fd, gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.
Power as rate of energy transfer, P = W/t.
Electricity generation from fossil fuels, nuclear, wind, water, geothermal and solar, with advantages and disadvantages (Physics only).

units.title: Solids, liquids and gases
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Density = mass / volume, and pressure = force / area.
Pressure in a fluid acts equally in all directions; pressure difference = h x density x g.
Change of state, particle arrangement, specific heat capacity and latent energy ideas (Physics only).
Gas pressure from random molecular motion; absolute zero and Kelvin conversion.
Pressure-temperature and pressure-volume relationships for a gas; p1/T1 = p2/T2 and p1V1 = p2V2.

units.title: Magnetism and electromagnetism
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Magnetic fields, magnetically hard and soft materials, induced magnetism, field line patterns.
A current produces a magnetic field; electromagnets and field of wire, coil and solenoid (Physics only).
Force on a current-carrying wire, the left-hand rule, d.c. motors and loudspeakers.
Electromagnetic induction and generators; factors that change the induced voltage.
Transformers, turns ratio, step-up and step-down use in transmission, Vp/Vs = np/ns (Physics only).

units.title: Radioactivity and particles
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Atomic structure, nuclear notation, atomic number, mass number and isotopes.
Alpha, beta and gamma radiation: ionisation, penetration, detection and background sources.
Nuclear equations balanced for mass and charge.
Activity in becquerels, half-life and half-life calculations, including graphs.
Uses of radioactivity, contamination against irradiation, and dangers of ionising radiation.
Fission chain reactions, control rods, moderator and shielding; fusion and its conditions.

units.title: Astrophysics
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: Galaxies, stars and the Solar System; gravitational field strength on other bodies.
Gravity and orbits of moons, planets, satellites and comets; orbital speed v = 2 pi r / T.
Stars classified by colour and surface temperature.
Life cycles of Sun-like stars and more massive stars.
Absolute magnitude and the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (Physics only).
Big Bang evidence, red-shift, cosmic microwave background and universal expansion (Physics only).

units.title: Natural hazards (3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
points: Define a natural hazard and distinguish the main types of hazard.
Explain why some hazards carry greater risk to people than others.
Factors affecting risk include vulnerability, capacity to cope and the nature of the hazard.

units.title: Tectonic hazards (3.1.1)
points: Describe plate tectonic theory and the structure of the Earth that supports it.
Locate earthquakes and volcanoes globally and link them to plate margins.
Explain how constructive, destructive and conservative margins produce earthquakes and volcanic activity.
Distinguish primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses.
Explain why people continue to live in tectonically active areas.
Evaluate monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as ways to reduce risk.
Case studies required: two named tectonic events, one in a high-income and one in a low-income country, compared.

units.title: Weather hazards (3.1.1)
points: Use the general atmospheric circulation model: pressure belts and surface winds.
Describe where tropical storms occur and link this to atmospheric circulation.
Explain how tropical storms form and develop, and describe their structure.
Discuss how climate change may alter their distribution, frequency and intensity.
Describe primary and secondary effects, and immediate and long-term responses.
Judge how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the effects.
Outline UK weather hazards and evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme.
Case studies required: one named tropical storm, and one recent UK extreme weather event with impacts and management.

units.title: Climate change (3.1.1)
points: Use evidence for climate change from the start of the Quaternary to the present.
Explain natural causes: orbital changes, volcanic activity and solar output.
Explain human causes: fossil fuel use, agriculture and deforestation.
Give an overview of effects on people and the environment.
Mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, tree planting and international agreements.
Adaptation: changing farming systems, managing water supply and reducing sea-level risk.

units.title: Ecosystems (3.1.2 The living world)
points: Explain producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling within an ecosystem.
Show how changing one component affects the balance of the whole system.
Describe the distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems (biomes).
Case study required: a small-scale UK ecosystem, such as a pond or woodland.

units.title: Tropical rainforests (3.1.2)
points: Describe physical characteristics and how climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people interrelate.
Explain plant and animal adaptations and issues of biodiversity.
Describe changing rates of deforestation and its causes (farming, logging, roads, mining, energy, settlement).
Assess impacts: economic development, soil erosion and contribution to climate change.
Explain the value of rainforests to people and the environment.
Evaluate sustainable management: selective logging, conservation, ecotourism, hardwood agreements and debt reduction.
Case study required: a named tropical rainforest area.

units.title: Hot deserts (3.1.2) - option, hot deserts or cold environments
points: Describe physical characteristics and the interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Explain adaptations of plants and animals, and biodiversity issues.
Opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, farming and tourism.
Challenges: extreme temperatures, water supply and inaccessibility.
Causes of desertification: climate change, population growth, fuelwood removal, overgrazing, over-cultivation, soil erosion.
Strategies to reduce desertification: water and soil management, tree planting, appropriate technology.
Case study required: a named hot desert area.

units.title: Cold environments (3.1.2) - option, hot deserts or cold environments
points: Describe physical characteristics and the links between climate, permafrost, soils, plants, animals and people.
Explain adaptations and biodiversity issues.
Opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, fishing and tourism.
Challenges: extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, and providing buildings and infrastructure.
Explain the value of cold environments as wilderness and why they need protection.
Evaluate strategies balancing development and conservation: technology, governments, treaties and conservation groups.
Case study required: a named cold environment.

units.title: UK physical landscapes (3.1.3 Physical landscapes in the UK)
points: Locate the major upland and lowland areas of the UK.
Locate the major river systems of the UK.
Apply this overview as the base for the chosen landscape studies.

units.title: Coastal landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe wave types and characteristics.
Explain weathering (mechanical, chemical), mass movement, erosion, longshore drift and deposition.
Explain how geology and rock type shape coastal forms.
Explain erosional landforms: headlands, bays, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks.
Explain depositional landforms: beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars.
Evaluate hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat, with costs and benefits.
Case studies required: a UK coastline with landforms, and a UK coastal management scheme.

units.title: River landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe the long profile and changing cross profile of a river and its valley.
Explain erosion, transportation and deposition processes in rivers.
Explain landforms: interlocking spurs, waterfalls, gorges, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, flood plains, estuaries.
Explain flood risk factors: precipitation, geology, relief and land use.
Interpret hydrographs showing the precipitation-discharge relationship.
Evaluate hard engineering (dams, straightening, embankments, relief channels) and soft engineering (warnings, zoning, tree planting, restoration).
Case studies required: a UK river valley with landforms, and a UK flood management scheme.

units.title: Glacial landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe the maximum extent of UK ice cover in the last ice age.
Explain freeze-thaw, plucking, abrasion, glacial movement and deposition.
Explain erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, troughs, ribbon lakes, hanging valleys.
Explain transport and deposition landforms: erratics, drumlins and moraines.
Describe economic activities in glaciated uplands: tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying.
Discuss land-use conflicts and tensions between development and conservation.
Case studies required: a UK glaciated upland with landforms, and one used for tourism with impacts and management.

units.title: Urban issues and challenges
points: Describe global urban change and the drivers of urbanisation: migration and natural increase.
Explain the rise of megacities and urban trends in high- and low-income countries.
Case study required: a major city in an LIC or NEE (location, growth, opportunities, challenges).
Challenges include slums, services, unemployment, pollution, congestion and waste.
Example required: urban planning that improves life for the urban poor.
Case study required: a major UK city (migration, opportunities, inequalities, sprawl and commuter settlements).
Example required: a UK urban regeneration project.
Describe sustainable urban living and traffic management strategies.

units.title: The changing economic world
points: Classify countries by development and quality of life; evaluate measures such as GNI, HDI and life expectancy.
Link the Demographic Transition Model to development.
Explain physical, economic and historical causes of uneven development, and the consequences.
Evaluate strategies to reduce the gap: investment, aid, Fairtrade, debt relief, microfinance, intermediate technology.
Example required: how tourism growth in an LIC or NEE reduces the development gap.
Case study required: one LIC or NEE (context, economy, TNCs, aid, environment, quality of life).
Explain UK economic change: de-industrialisation, globalisation, post-industrial economy and policy.
Example required: how modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable.
Discuss rural change, the north-south divide, and the UK's trade, cultural and political links.

units.title: Resource management (3.2.3 The challenge of resource management) - compulsory
points: Explain the importance of food, water and energy for wellbeing.
Describe global inequalities in resource supply and consumption.
Explain changing UK demand and provision for food, water and energy.
Food: demand for imports, seasonal and organic food, food miles, local sourcing, agribusiness.
Water: changing demand, water quality, and matching supply to surplus and deficit areas.
Energy: the changing energy mix, fossil fuel decline and growth of renewables.

units.title: Food (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global food surplus and deficit and calorie supply.
Explain rising consumption and the supply factors affecting food security.
Assess impacts of insecurity: famine, undernutrition, soil erosion, price rises and unrest.
Evaluate strategies: irrigation, hydroponics, new green revolution, biotechnology, appropriate technology.
Example required: a large-scale agricultural development with pros and cons.
Explain sustainable options: organic farming, permaculture, urban farming, waste reduction.
Example required: a local scheme in an LIC or NEE increasing sustainable food supply.

units.title: Water (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global water surplus and deficit patterns.
Explain rising consumption and supply factors: climate, geology, pollution, over-abstraction, poverty.
Assess impacts of insecurity: disease, pollution, reduced output and conflict.
Evaluate supply strategies: diversion, storage, dams and reservoirs, transfers, desalination.
Example required: a large-scale water transfer scheme with advantages and disadvantages.
Explain sustainable options: conservation, groundwater management, recycling and grey water.
Example required: a local scheme in an LIC or NEE increasing sustainable water supply.

units.title: Energy (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global distribution of energy consumption and supply.
Explain rising consumption and supply factors: geography, cost, technology and politics.
Assess impacts of insecurity on sensitive areas, economies, environment and conflict.
Compare renewable sources and non-renewable sources including fossil fuels and nuclear.
Example required: extraction of a fossil fuel with advantages and disadvantages.
Explain sustainable options: energy conservation, sustainable design, demand reduction, cleaner fossil fuel technology.
Example required: a local renewable energy scheme in an LIC or NEE.

units.title: Issue evaluation
points: Study a contemporary geographical issue drawn from compulsory content, shown through a pre-release booklet.
The booklet is issued 12 weeks before the exam; a clean copy is given in the exam.
Sources may include maps, graphs, statistics, photographs, satellite images and stakeholder statements.
Link physical (3.1) and human (3.2) themes across several scales.
Weigh stakeholders' views, advantages and disadvantages, and alternative options.
Make and justify a decision in an extended evaluative answer.

units.title: Fieldwork
points: Complete two geographical enquiries using primary data collected in the field.
The enquiries must be in two contrasting environments, with at least two outside-school visits.
Both physical and human geography must be covered, and at least one must show their interaction.
Know the six enquiry stages: question, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusions, evaluation.
Choose and justify sampling methods and assess risks in the field.
Present and analyse data using suitable graphical, cartographic and statistical techniques.
Evaluate method, reliability and the limits of conclusions.
The school submits a signed fieldwork statement; students state their own enquiry titles in the exam.

units.title: Geographical skills
points: Cartographic: atlas and OS maps, grid references, distance, direction, gradient, relief, photographs, sketch maps.
Graphical: choose, draw and read bar, line, pie, histogram, scatter, pyramid, choropleth, isoline and flow-line maps.
Numerical: number, area, scale, ratio, proportion, frequency and data-sheet design.
Statistical: averages, spread, cumulative frequency, percentage change, percentiles and misleading presentation.
Use qualitative and quantitative data, including GIS and satellite imagery.
Enquiry and argument: frame questions and build evidenced conclusions.
Literacy: communicate clearly in writing for different audiences.

units.title: Personal aspects of the Prophet's life
points: Ancestry and the main events of his early years, from birth to parenthood.
Early influences, including his parents, Abu Talib and Bahira.
His work and business before the revelation of the Qur'an.
His relationships with his wives and children.
Why his early life mattered for his later work as Allah's messenger.

units.title: The Revelation of the Qur'an
points: The events of the Night of Power (Night of Decree).
Details of the conversation with Jibrail in the cave at Hira.
Why this experience mattered in the establishment of Islam.
The importance of the revelation of the Qur'an to Muslims.
How the Qur'an was compiled.

units.title: The Prophethood of Muhammad
points: The meaning of the title 'Seal of the Prophets'.
The importance of Muhammad's role as prophet in establishing Islam.
The opposition faced in Makkah by the Prophet and his followers.

units.title: Opposition and Hijrah
points: The events of the boycott and the Mi'raj.
The plot to kill the Prophet and the details of the flight to Madinah.
The welcome by the people of Madinah and the building of mosques there.
The significance of the Hijrah for the Prophet and the early community.
Support given to the Prophet by Abu Bakr, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Uthman and Umar.
The contribution of the Companions and the helpers (Ansar) to establishing Islam.

units.title: The Sunnah of the Prophet
points: The importance for Muslims of his teachings, deeds and sayings.
How the Sunnah was recorded.
The role of the Sunnah in establishing Islamic belief and practice.

units.title: Teachings and example of the Prophet on justice and equality
points: His teaching and example on social and economic justice.
His teaching and example on human rights.
His relationship with people of other religions.
His teaching on respect for mothers and for women.
What these teachings show about Muslim beliefs about society.

units.title: The Prophet as leader
points: His role in the establishment of the Shari'ah.
The consolidation and expansion of Islam after the Hijrah.
His treatment of opponents and prisoners.
His relationship with other communities and countries.

units.title: Battles fought by the Prophet
points: The battles fought after the Hijrah: Badr, Ohud, the Trench and Khyber.
The reasons the Prophet chose to fight each battle.
The importance of the battles for the establishment of Islam.

units.title: The Prophet's final acts and his achievements
points: His final pilgrimage and sermon.
The main themes and importance of his example and teaching in his later years.
His significant achievements in society, religion and politics.
The events at his death in Madinah.

units.title: The nature of belief in Allah
points: The meaning and importance of belief in the oneness of Allah (Tawhid).
The attributes of Allah: omnipotence, creator, merciful and just.
The meaning and importance of teaching about shirk and nifaq (hypocrisy).
The characteristics of Allah as shown in the Qur'an.

units.title: Risalah
points: The nature and importance of prophethood for Muslims.
What the roles of prophets teach Muslims.
The lives of earlier prophets: Adam, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Musa, Dawud and Isa.

units.title: The holy books of Islam
points: The nature of the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and the Scrolls of Abraham.
The importance of these holy books in the establishment of Islam.

units.title: al-Qadr
points: The nature and importance of predestination for Muslims.
How al-Qadr and free will relate to the Day of Judgment.
The significance of belief in al-Qadr for the early Islamic community.
The nature and significance of evil and suffering.

units.title: Akhirah
points: Teachings about life after death: the final judgment.
Paradise (Jannah) and hell (Jahannam).
Life in the grave and Barzakh.
How these teachings are expressed in the Qur'an.

units.title: Malaikah
points: The nature and importance of angels for Muslims.
The roles and importance of Jibrail, Mikail, Israfil and Izrael.

units.title: Shari'ah
points: The principal sources of Shari'ah law: the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
The importance of the Shari'ah in the early Islamic community.
Related sources of law: ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).
The difference between halal and haram in Muslim acts.
The five categories: fard, mandub, mubah, makruh and haram.

units.title: Islamic etiquette, attitude and manners
points: Islamic etiquette in relations with other people.
Islamic attitudes to lying and harmful speech.
Islamic manners when eating.
Why correct etiquette matters, with support from the Qur'an and Sunnah.

units.title: The early leaders of the Muslim community
points: Leadership of Islam after the death of the Prophet.
The role and achievements of the early leaders.
The importance of the period of the early leaders for the Islamic community.

units.title: Shahadah
points: The nature and role of Shahadah for Muslims.
The importance of reciting the Shahadah.
How the Shahadah is used in practice.

units.title: Salah
points: The nature, significance and importance of Salah in Muslim life.
How Salah is performed: ablution, times, directions, movements and recitations.
Salah in the home, in the mosque and at Friday (Jummah) prayer.
Exemptions from Salah.

units.title: Sawm
points: The nature, role, significance and purpose of fasting in Ramadan.
Those who are exempt from fasting.
The importance of Laylat al-Qadr for Muslims today.

units.title: Zakah and Khums
points: The nature and purpose of Zakah.
The nature and purpose of Khums.
The importance of Zakah and Khums for Muslims.
The global importance of giving support to those in need.

units.title: Hajj
points: The nature, role, origins and significance of Hajj.
Key actions performed during Hajj.
The importance of Hajj for Muslims.
Benefits and challenges of attending Hajj.
Exemptions from performing Hajj.

units.title: Jihad
points: The origins, meaning and significance of jihad in Islam.
The distinction between the greater (inner) and lesser (outer) jihad.
The importance of the greater jihad in Muslim life.
Conditions for declaring lesser jihad, with reference to Surah 2:190-194 and 22:39.

units.title: Islamic festivals
points: The origins and activities of Eid-ul-Adha, Eid-ul-Fitr and Ashura.
The meaning and significance of the festivals for Muslims.

units.title: Marriage and the family
points: The significance of marriage in Islamic life.
Muslim teachings about marriage.
Muslim teachings about the purpose of families.
Ceremonies relating to birth and death, and their meaning.
The importance of procreation in strengthening the Ummah.

units.title: Muslim citizenship and religious and political leadership
points: Muslim beliefs about leadership and the responsibility of religious and political leaders.
The challenges faced by leaders of Islam in the modern world.
The challenges and responsibilities of citizenship for Muslims.
The Prophet and his successors as models of leadership.

units.title: Number: structure and calculation
points: Order integers, decimals and fractions, including negatives, using the comparison symbols (N1).
Apply the four operations to integers, decimals and fractions of any sign, using place value (N2).
Use inverse operations, cancellation and the order of operations including powers, roots and reciprocals (N3).
Use primes, factors, multiples, HCF, LCM and prime factorisation (N4).
Apply systematic listing; at Higher also the product rule for counting (N5).
Use positive integer powers and real roots, and estimate powers and roots (N6).
Calculate with roots and integer indices; at Higher include fractional indices (N7).
Calculate exactly with fractions and multiples of pi; at Higher use and rationalise surds (N8).
Calculate with and interpret numbers in standard form (N9).

units.title: Number: fractions, decimals and percentages
points: Convert between terminating decimals and fractions; at Higher also recurring decimals (N10).
Work with fractions within ratio problems (N11).
Interpret and use fractions and percentages as operators (N12).

units.title: Number: measures and accuracy
points: Use standard units of measure, including compound measures (N13).
Estimate answers and check calculations, including those made with technology (N14).
Round to appropriate accuracy and use inequality notation for error intervals (N15).
Apply and interpret limits of accuracy; at Higher use upper and lower bounds (N16).

units.title: Algebra: notation, vocabulary and manipulation
points: Use algebraic notation correctly, including indices, fractional coefficients and brackets (A1).
Substitute into expressions and formulae, including scientific formulae (A2).
Use the vocabulary of expressions, equations, formulae, identities, inequalities, terms and factors (A3).
Simplify, expand and factorise; at Higher expand several binomials and factorise ax^2 + bx + c (A4).
Use standard formulae and rearrange to change the subject (A5).
Distinguish equations from identities; at Higher construct algebraic proofs (A6).
Treat expressions as functions; at Higher use inverse and composite functions with f(x) notation (A7).

units.title: Algebra: graphs (linear, quadratic and standard curves)
points: Work with coordinates in all four quadrants (A8).
Plot straight-line graphs; use y = mx + c, parallel lines, and equations from two points (A9).
At Higher identify perpendicular lines and their gradients (A9).
Interpret gradients and intercepts of linear functions graphically and numerically (A10).
Find roots, intercepts and turning points of quadratics; at Higher use completing the square (A11).
Recognise and sketch linear, quadratic, cubic and reciprocal graphs (A12).
At Higher also sketch exponential graphs and sine, cosine and tangent graphs (A12).

units.title: Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
points: Sketch translations and reflections of a given function (A13, Higher only).
Plot and interpret graphs from real contexts, such as distance-time and velocity-time (A14).
At Higher include reciprocal and exponential graphs in context (A14).
Estimate gradients and areas under non-linear graphs and interpret them, without calculus (A15, Higher only).
Use the equation of a circle centred on the origin and find a tangent at a point (A16, Higher only).

units.title: Algebra: linear and quadratic equations
points: Solve linear equations, including unknowns on both sides and with brackets or fractions (A17).
Approximate solutions to equations using graphs (A17).
Solve quadratics by factorising and estimate roots from graphs (A18).
At Higher also solve quadratics by completing the square and the quadratic formula (A18).

units.title: Algebra: simultaneous equations and iteration
points: Solve two linear simultaneous equations algebraically and graphically (A19).
At Higher solve a linear and a quadratic simultaneous pair algebraically (A19).
Find approximate solutions to equations using iteration (A20, Higher only).

units.title: Algebra: forming equations and inequalities
points: Translate situations into equations, solve them and interpret the solution (A21).
Solve linear inequalities in one variable and show them on a number line (A22).
At Higher cover inequalities in two variables, quadratic inequalities, set notation and regions on graphs (A22).

units.title: Algebra: sequences
points: Generate terms using term-to-term and position-to-term rules (A23).
Recognise triangular, square, cube, arithmetic, Fibonacci-type, quadratic and geometric sequences (A24).
At Higher geometric sequences may have surd ratios (A24).
Find the nth term of linear sequences; at Higher also quadratic sequences (A25).

units.title: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
points: Convert between related standard and compound units in numerical and algebraic contexts (R1).
Use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (R2).
Write one quantity as a fraction of another, including fractions above 1 (R3).
Use ratio notation, simplify ratios and share in a given ratio (R4, R5).
Express a multiplicative relationship as a ratio or fraction (R6).
Use proportion as equality of ratios and link ratio to fractions and linear functions (R7, R8).

units.title: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
points: Use percentages above 100%, percentage change, reverse percentages and simple interest (R9).
Solve direct and inverse proportion problems using graphs and algebra (R10).
Use compound units: speed, pay rates, unit pricing, density and pressure (R11).
Compare lengths, areas and volumes using ratio, linked to similarity and scale factors (R12).

units.title: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
points: Understand inverse proportion as X proportional to 1/Y; at Higher construct the equations (R13).
Interpret the gradient of a straight-line graph as a rate of change (R14).
Recognise graphs of direct and inverse proportion (R14).
Interpret the gradient at a point on a curve as an instantaneous rate of change, using tangents (R15, Higher only).
Solve growth and decay problems, including compound interest; at Higher general iterative processes (R16).

units.title: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
points: Use geometric vocabulary and notation, and draw diagrams from descriptions (G1).
Use ruler and compass constructions and solve loci problems (G2).
Apply angle facts at a point, on a line, in parallel lines, triangles and polygons (G3).
Use properties of quadrilaterals and other plane figures (G4).
Use congruence criteria SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS (G5).
Use angle, congruence and similarity properties to derive results and simple proofs (G6).
Describe and construct congruent and similar shapes by transformation; at Higher use negative scale factors (G7).
At Higher describe how combinations of rotations, reflections and translations affect shapes (G8).

units.title: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
points: Identify and use circle parts: chord, tangent, arc, sector and segment (G9).
Apply and prove standard circle theorems (G10, Higher only).
Solve geometry problems on coordinate axes (G11).
Identify faces, surfaces, edges and vertices of 3D solids (G12).
Construct and interpret plans and elevations of 3D shapes (G13).
Use standard measurement units and related concepts (G14).

units.title: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
points: Measure lines and angles; use maps, scale drawings and bearings (G15).
Use area formulae for triangles, parallelograms, trapezia, and volume of prisms including cylinders (G16).
Use circle formulae; find surface areas and volumes of spheres, pyramids, cones and composite solids (G17).
Calculate arc lengths, angles and sector areas (G18).
Apply similarity to lengths; at Higher to areas and volumes (G19).

units.title: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
points: Use Pythagoras and sine, cosine and tangent in right-angled triangles (G20).
At Higher extend Pythagoras and trigonometry to 3D figures (G20).
Know exact trigonometric values for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees (G21).
Use the sine rule and cosine rule to find lengths and angles (G22, Higher only).
Use the area formula one half ab sin C for any triangle (G23, Higher only).

units.title: Geometry and measures: vectors
points: Describe translations as 2D column vectors (G24).
Add, subtract and scalar-multiply vectors using diagrams and column notation (G25).
At Higher use vectors in geometric arguments and proofs (G25).

units.title: Probability
points: Record and analyse outcome frequencies using tables and frequency trees (P1).
Use randomness, fairness and equally likely outcomes; link expected frequency to probability (P2, P3).
Know that probabilities of exhaustive, mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1 (P4).
Understand that larger unbiased samples tend towards the theoretical probability (P5).
List outcomes systematically with tables, grids, Venn diagrams and tree diagrams (P6, P7).
Calculate probabilities of independent and dependent combined events, stating assumptions (P8).
At Higher calculate conditional probabilities using two-way tables, trees and Venn diagrams (P9).

units.title: Statistics
points: Infer properties of a population from samples, recognising limitations of sampling (S1).
Construct and interpret tables, charts and diagrams for categorical, discrete data and time series (S2).
Construct and interpret histograms with unequal class widths and cumulative frequency graphs (S3, Higher only).
Compare distributions using suitable graphs and averages and spread (S4).
At Higher use box plots, quartiles and interquartile range (S4).
Use statistics to describe a population (S5).
Interpret scatter graphs, correlation and lines of best fit, noting the risks of extrapolation (S6).
